entries.116a674c418847d27a5bc61c506c25e60f808a86: <div sID="gen10122" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="35" osisID="Job.35" sID="Job.35"/> <div eID="gen10122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10123" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10124" type="x-p"/> Job being still silent, Elihu follows his blow, and here, a third time, undertakes to show him that he had spoken amiss, and ought to recant. Three improper sayings he here charges him with, and returns answer to them distinctly:—I. He had represented religion as an indifferent unprofitable thing, which God enjoins for his own sake, not for ours; Elihu evinces the contrary, <reference osisRef="Job.35.1-Job.35.8">ver. 1-8</reference>. II. He had complained of God as deaf to the cries of the oppressed, against which imputation Elihu here justifies God, <reference osisRef="Job.35.9-Job.35.13">ver. 9-13</reference>. III. He had despaired of the return of God's favour to him, because it was so long deferred, but Elihu shows him the true cause of the delay, <reference osisRef="Job.35.14-Job.35.16">ver. 14-16</reference>.
entries.77fd6f67d5c833634fb11845a0bb4d78561b5212: <div eID="gen10124" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10123" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Address of Elihu. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen10125" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Elihu spake moreover, and said, <hi type="super">2</hi> Thinkest thou this to be right, <hi type="italic">that</hi> thou saidst, My righteousness <hi type="italic">is</hi> more than God's? <hi type="super">3</hi> For thou saidst, What advantage will it be unto thee? <hi type="italic">and,</hi> What profit shall I have, <hi type="italic">if I be cleansed</hi> from my sin? <hi type="super">4</hi> I will answer thee, and thy companions with thee. <hi type="super">5</hi> Look unto the heavens, and see; and behold the clouds <hi type="italic">which</hi> are higher than thou. 6 If thou sinnest, what doest thou against him? or <hi type="italic">if</hi> thy transgressions be multiplied, what doest thou unto him? <hi type="super">7</hi> If thou be righteous, what givest thou him? or what receiveth he of thine hand? <hi type="super">8</hi> Thy wickedness <hi type="italic">may hurt</hi> a man as thou <hi type="italic">art;</hi> and thy righteousness <hi type="italic">may profit</hi> the son of man. <div eID="gen10125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10126" type="x-p"/> We have here, <div eID="gen10126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10127" type="x-p"/> I. The bad words which Elihu charges upon Job, <reference osisRef="Job.35.2-Job.35.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. To evince the badness of them he appeals to Job himself, and his own sober thoughts, in the reflection: <hi type="italic">Thinkest thou this to be right?</hi> This intimates Elihu's confidence that the reproof he now gave was just, for he could refer the judgment of it even to Job himself. Those that have truth and equity on their side sooner or later will have every man's conscience on their side. It also intimates his good opinion of Job, that he thought better than he spoke, and that, though he had spoken amiss, yet, when he perceived his mistake, he would not stand to it. When we have said, in our haste, that which was not right, it becomes us to own that our second thoughts convince us that it was wrong. Two things Elihu here reproves Job for:—1. For justifying himself more than God, which was the thing that first provoked him, <reference osisRef="Job.32.2">ch. xxxii. 2</reference>. "Thou hast, in effect, said, <hi type="italic">My righteousness is more than God's,</hi>" that is, "I have done more for God than ever he did for me; so that, when the accounts are balanced, he will be brought in debtor to me." As if Job thought his services had been paid less than they deserved and his sins punished more than they deserved, which is a most unjust and wicked thought for any man to harbour and especially to utter. When Job insisted so much upon his own integrity, and the severity of God's dealings with him, he did in effect say, <hi type="italic">My righteousness is more than God's;</hi> whereas, though we be ever so good and our afflictions ever so great, we are chargeable with unrighteousness and God is not. 2. For disowning the benefits and advantages of religion because he suffered these things: <hi type="italic">What profit shall I have if I be cleansed from my sin?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.35.3">v. 3</reference>. This is gathered from <reference osisRef="Job.9.30-Job.9.31">ch. ix. 30, 31</reference>. <hi type="italic">Though I make my hands ever so clean,</hi> what the nearer am I? <hi type="italic">Thou shalt plunge me in the ditch.</hi> And <reference osisRef="Job.10.15">ch. x. 15</reference>, <hi type="italic">If I be wicked, woe to me;</hi> but, if I be righteous, it is all the same. The psalmist, when he compared his own afflictions with the prosperity of the wicked, was tempted to say, <hi type="italic">Verily I have cleansed my heart in vain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.73.13">Ps. lxxiii. 13</reference>. And, if Job said so, he did in effect say, <hi type="italic">My righteousness is more than God's</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.35.9">v. 9</reference>); for, if he got nothing by his religion, God was more beholden to him than he was to God. But, though there might be some colour for it, yet it was not fair to charge these words upon Job, when he himself had made them the wicked words of prospering sinners (<reference osisRef="Job.21.15">ch. xxi. 15</reference>, <hi type="italic">What profit shall we have if we pray to him?</hi>) and had immediately disclaimed them. <hi type="italic">The counsel of the wicked is far from me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.21.16">ch. xxi. 16</reference>. It is not a fair way of disputing to charge men with those consequences of their opinions which they expressly renounce. <div eID="gen10127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10128" type="x-p"/> II. The good answer which Elihu gives to this (<reference osisRef="Job.35.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will</hi> undertake to <hi type="italic">answer thee, and thy companions with thee,</hi>" that is, "all those that approve thy sayings and are ready to justify thee in them, and all others that say as thou sayest: "I have that to offer which will silence them all." To do this he has recourse to his old maxim (<reference osisRef="Job.33.12">ch. xxxiii. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">that God is greater than man.</hi> This is a truth which, if duly improved, will serve many good purposes, and particularly this to prove that God is debtor to no man. The greatest of men may be a debtor to the meanest; but such is the infinite disproportion between God and man that the great God cannot possibly receive any benefit by man, and therefore cannot be supposed to lie under any obligation to man; for, if he be obliged by his purpose and promise, it is only to himself. That is a challenge which no man can take up (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.35">Rom. xi. 35</reference>), <hi type="italic">Who hath first given to God,</hi> let him prove it, <hi type="italic">and it shall be recompensed to him again.</hi> Why should we demand it, as a just debt, to gain by our religion (as Job seemed to do), when the God we serve does not gain by it? 1. Elihu needs not prove that God is above man; it is agreed by all; but he endeavours to affect Job and us with it, by an ocular demonstration of the height of the heavens and the clouds, <reference osisRef="Job.35.5">v. 5</reference>. They are far above us, and God is far above them; how much then is he set out of the reach either of our sins or of our services! <hi type="italic">Look unto the heavens, and behold the clouds.</hi> God made man erect, <hi type="italic">coelumque tueri jussit—and bade him look up to heaven.</hi> Idolaters looked up, and worshipped the hosts of heaven, the sun, moon, and stars; but we must look up to heaven, and worship the Lord of those hosts. They are higher than we, but God is infinitely above them. His <hi type="italic">glory is above the heavens</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.8.1">Ps. viii. 1</reference>) and the knowledge of him higher than heaven, <reference osisRef="Job.11.8">ch. xi. 8</reference>. 2. But hence he infers that God is not affected, either one way or other, by any thing that we do. (1.) He owns that men may be either bettered or damaged by what we do (<reference osisRef="Job.35.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thy wickedness,</hi> perhaps, may <hi type="italic">hurt a man as thou art,</hi> may occasion him trouble in his outward concerns. A wicked man may wound, or rob, or slander his neighbour, or may draw him into sin and so prejudice his soul. Thy righteousness, thy justice, thy charity, thy wisdom, thy piety, may perhaps <hi type="italic">profit the son of man.</hi> Our goodness <hi type="italic">extends to the saints that are in the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.16.3">Ps. xvi. 3</reference>. To men like ourselves we are in a capacity either of doing injury or of showing kindness; and in both these the sovereign Lord and Judge of all will interest himself, will reward those that do good and punish those that do hurt to their fellow-creatures and fellow-subjects. But, (2.) He utterly denies that God can really be either prejudiced or advantaged by what any, even the greatest men of the earth, do, or can do. [1.] The sins of the worst sinners are no damage to him (<reference osisRef="Job.35.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">If thou sinnest</hi> wilfully, and of malice prepense, against him, with a high hand, nay, <hi type="italic">if thy transgressions be multiplied,</hi> and the acts of sin be ever so often repeated, yet <hi type="italic">what doest thou against him?</hi>" This is a challenge to the carnal mind, and defies the most daring sinner to do his worst. It speaks much for the greatness and glory of God that it is not in the power of his worst enemies to do him any real prejudice. Sin is said to <hi type="italic">be against God</hi> because so the sinner intends it and so God takes it, and it is an injury to his honour; yet it cannot <hi type="italic">do any thing against him.</hi> The malice of sinners is impotent malice: it cannot destroy his being or perfections, cannot dethrone him from his power and dominion, cannot disturb his peace and repose, cannot defeat his counsels and designs, nor can it derogate from his essential glory. Job therefore spoke amiss in saying <hi type="italic">What profit is it that I am cleansed from my sin?</hi> God was no gainer by his reformation; and who then would gain if he himself did not? [2.] The services of the best saints are no profit to him (<reference osisRef="Job.35.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">If thou be righteous, what givest thou to him?</hi> He needs not our service; or, if he did want to have the work done, he has better hands than ours at command. Our religion brings no accession at all to his felicity. He is so far from being beholden to us that we are beholden to him for making us righteous and accepting our righteousness; and therefore we can demand nothing from him, nor have any reason to complain if we have not what we expect, but to be thankful that we have better than we deserve.
entries.aa660d2d39afdf33581da1fec7073ced5be1248d: <div eID="gen10128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10129" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> By reason of the multitude of oppressions they make <hi type="italic">the oppressed</hi> to cry: they cry out by reason of the arm of the mighty. <hi type="super">10</hi> But none saith, Where <hi type="italic">is</hi> God my maker, who giveth songs in the night; <hi type="super">11</hi> Who teacheth us more than the beasts of the earth, and maketh us wiser than the fowls of heaven? <hi type="super">12</hi> There they cry, but none giveth answer, because of the pride of evil men. <hi type="super">13</hi> Surely God will not hear vanity, neither will the Almighty regard it. <div eID="gen10129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10130" type="x-p"/> Elihu here returns an answer to another word that Job had said, which, he thought, reflected much upon the justice and goodness of God, and therefore ought not to pass without a remark. Observe, <div eID="gen10130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10131" type="x-p"/> I. What it was that Job complained of; it was this, That God did not regard the cries of the oppressed against their oppressors (<reference osisRef="Job.35.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">By reason of the multitude of oppressions,</hi> the many hardships which proud tyrants put upon poor people and the barbarous usage they give them, <hi type="italic">they make the oppressed to cry;</hi> but it is to no purpose: God does not appear to right them. They cry out, they cry on still, <hi type="italic">by reason of the arm of the mighty,</hi> which lies heavily upon them." This seems to refer to those words of Job (<reference osisRef="Job.24.12">ch. xxiv. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">Men groan from out of the city, and the soul of the wounded cries out</hi> against the oppressors, <hi type="italic">yet God lays not folly to them,</hi> does not reckon with them for it. This is a thing that Job knows not what to make of, nor how to reconcile to the justice of God and his government. <hi type="italic">Is there a righteous God, and can it be that he should so slowly hear, so slowly see?</hi> <div eID="gen10131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10132" type="x-p"/> II. How Elihu solves the difficulty. If the cries of the oppressed be not heard, the fault is not in God; he is ready to hear and help them. But the fault is in themselves; they <hi type="italic">ask and have not,</hi> but it is <hi type="italic">because they ask amiss,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.4.3">James iv. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">They cry out by reason of the arm of the mighty,</hi> but it is a complaining cry, a wailing cry, not a penitent praying cry, the cry of nature and passion, not of grace. See <reference osisRef="Hos.7.14">Hos. vii. 14,</reference>, <hi type="italic">They have not cried unto me with their heart when they howled upon their beds.</hi> How then can we expect that they should be answered and relieved? <div eID="gen10132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10133" type="x-p"/> 1. They do not enquire after God, nor seek to acquaint themselves with him, under their affliction (<reference osisRef="Job.35.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">But none saith, Where is God my Maker?</hi> Afflictions are sent to direct and quicken us to <hi type="italic">enquire early after God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.78.34">Ps. lxxxviii. 34</reference>. But many that groan under great oppressions never mind God, nor take notice of his hand in their troubles; if they did, they would bear their troubles more patiently and be more benefited by them. Of the many that are afflicted and oppressed, few get the good they might get by their affliction. It should drive them to God, but how seldom is this the case! It is lamentable to see so little religion among the poor and miserable part of mankind. Every one complains of his troubles; <hi type="italic">but none saith, Where is God my Maker?</hi> that is, none repent of their sins, none return to him that smites them, none seek the face and favour of God, and that comfort in him which would balance their outward afflictions. They are wholly taken up with the wretchedness of their condition, as if that would excuse them in living without God in the world which should engage them to cleave the more closely to him. Observe, (1.) God is our Maker, the author of our being, and, under that notion, it concerns us to regard and remember him, <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.1">Eccl. xii. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">God my makers,</hi> in the plural number, which some think is, if not an indication, yet an intimation, of the Trinity of persons in the unity of the Godhead. <hi type="italic">Let us make man.</hi> (2.) It is our duty therefore to enquire after him. Where is he, that we may pay our homage to him, may own our dependence upon him and obligations to him? Where is he, that we may apply to him for maintenance and protection, may receive law from him, and may seek our happiness in his favour, from whose power we received our being? (3.) It is to be lamented that he is so little enquired after by the children of men. All are asking, Where is mirth? Where is wealth? Where is a good bargain? But none ask, <hi type="italic">Where is God my Maker?</hi> <div eID="gen10133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10134" type="x-p"/> 2. They do not take notice of the mercies they enjoy in and under their afflictions, nor are thankful for them, and therefore cannot expect that God should deliver them out of their afflictions. (1.) He provides for our inward comfort and joy under our outward troubles, and we ought to make use of that, and wait his time for the removal of our troubles: He <hi type="italic">gives songs in the night,</hi> that is, when our condition is ever so dark, and sad, and melancholy, there is that in God, in his providence and promise, which is sufficient, not only to support us, but to fill us with joy and consolation, and enable us in every thing to give thanks, and even to rejoice in tribulation. When we only pore upon the afflictions we are under, and neglect the consolations of God which are treasured up for us, it is just with God to reject our prayers. (2.) He preserves to us the use of our reason and understanding (<reference osisRef="Job.35.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Who teaches us more than the beasts of the earth,</hi> that is, who has endued us with more noble powers and faculties than they are endued with and has made us capable of more excellent pleasures and employments here and for ever. Now this comes in here, [1.] As that which furnishes us with matter for thanksgiving, even under the heaviest burden of affliction. Whatever we are deprived of, we have our immortal souls, those jewels of more worth than all the world, continued to us; even those that kill the body cannot hurt <hi type="italic">them.</hi> And if our affliction prevail not to disturb the exercise of their faculties, but we enjoy the use of our reason and the peace of our consciences, we have much reason to be thankful, how pressing soever our calamities otherwise are. [2.] As a reason why we should, under our afflictions, enquire after God our Maker, and seek unto him. This is the greatest excellency of reason, that it makes us capable of religion, and it is in that especially that we are <hi type="italic">taught more than the beasts and the fowls.</hi> They have wonderful instincts and sagacities in seeking out their food, their physic, their shelter; but none of them are capable of enquiring, <hi type="italic">Where is God my Maker?</hi> Something like logic, and philosophy, and politics, has been observed among the brute-creatures, but never any thing of divinity or religion; these are peculiar to man. If therefore the oppressed only <hi type="italic">cry by reason of the arm of the mighty,</hi> and do not look up to God, they do no more than the brutes (who complain when they are hurt), and they forget that instruction and wisdom by which they are advanced so far above them. God relieves the brute-creatures because they cry to him according to the best of their capacity, <reference osisRef="Job.38.41">ch. xxxviii. 41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.104.21">Ps. civ. 21</reference>. But what reason have men to expect relief, who are capable of enquiring after God as their Maker and yet cry to him no otherwise than as brutes do? <div eID="gen10134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10135" type="x-p"/> 3. They are proud and unhumbled under their afflictions, which were sent to mortify them and to hide pride from them (<reference osisRef="Job.35.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">There they cry</hi>—there they lie exclaiming against their oppressors, and filling the ears of all about them with their complaints, not sparing to reflect upon God himself and his providence—<hi type="italic">but none gives answer.</hi> God does not work deliverance for them, and perhaps men do not much regard them; and why so? It is <hi type="italic">because of the pride of evil men;</hi> they are evil men; they <hi type="italic">regard iniquity in their hearts,</hi> and therefore God will not hear their prayers, <reference osisRef="Ps.66.18">Ps. lxvi. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.15">Isa. i. 15</reference>. <hi type="italic">God hears not</hi> such <hi type="italic">sinners.</hi> They have, it may be, brought themselves into trouble by their own wickedness; they are the devil's poor; and then who can pity them? Yet this is not all: they are proud still, and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> they do not seek unto God (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.4">Ps. x. 4</reference>), or, if they do cry unto him, <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> he does not give answer, for he hears only the <hi type="italic">desire of the humble</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.17">Ps. x. 17</reference>) and delivers those by his providence whom he has first by his grace prepared and made fit for deliverance, which we are not if, under humbling afflictions, our hearts remain unhumbled and our pride unmortified. The case is plain then, If we cry to God for the removal of the oppression and affliction we are under, and it is not removed, the reason is not because the Lord's hand is shortened or his ear heavy, but because the affliction has not done its work; we are not sufficiently humbled, and therefore must thank ourselves that it is continued. <div eID="gen10135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10136" type="x-p"/> 4. They are not sincere, and upright, and inward with God, in their supplications to him, and therefore he does not hear and answer them (<reference osisRef="Job.35.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">God will not hear vanity,</hi> that is, the hypocritical prayer, which is a vain prayer, coming out of feigned lips. It is a vanity to think that God should hear it, who searches the heart and requires <hi type="italic">truth in the inward part.</hi>
entries.eafd7405744ac62e9c9fe553205457877b82b319: <div eID="gen10136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10137" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> Although thou sayest thou shalt not see him, <hi type="italic">yet</hi> judgment <hi type="italic">is</hi> before him; therefore trust thou in him. <hi type="super">15</hi> But now, because <hi type="italic">it is</hi> not <hi type="italic">so,</hi> he hath visited in his anger; yet he knoweth <hi type="italic">it</hi> not in great extremity: <hi type="super">16</hi> Therefore doth Job open his mouth in vain; he multiplieth words without knowledge. <div eID="gen10137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10138" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Another improper word for which Elihu reproves Job (<reference osisRef="Job.35.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou sayest thou shalt not see him;</hi> that is, 1. "Thou complainest that thou dost not understand the meaning of his severe dealings with thee, nor discern the drift and design of them," <reference osisRef="Job.23.8-Job.23.9">ch. xxiii. 8, 9</reference>. And, 2. "Thou despairest of seeing his gracious returns to thee, of seeing better days again, and art ready to give up all for gone;" as Hezekiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.11">Isa. xxxviii. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">I shall not see the Lord.</hi> As, when we are in prosperity, we are ready to think our mountain will never be brought low, so when we are in adversity we are ready to think our valley will never be filled, but, in both, to conclude that <hi type="italic">to morrow must be as this day,</hi> which is as absurd as to think, when the weather is either fair or foul, that is will be always so, that the flowing tide will always flow, or the ebbing tide will always ebb. <div eID="gen10138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10139" type="x-p"/> II. The answer which Elihu gives to this despairing word that Job had said, which is this, 1. That, when he looked up to God, he had no just reason to speak thus despairingly: <hi type="italic">Judgment is before him,</hi> that is, "He knows what he has to do, and will do all in infinite wisdom and justice; he has the entire plan and model of providence before him, and knows what he will do, which we do not, and therefore we understand not what he does. There is a day of judgment before him, when all the seeming disorders of providence will be set to rights and the dark chapters of it will be expounded. Then thou shalt see the full meaning of these dark events, and the final period of these dismal events; then thou shalt see his face with joy; <hi type="italic">therefore trust in him,</hi> depend upon him, wait for him, and believe that the issue will be good at last." When we consider that God is infinitely wise, and righteous, and faithful, and that he is a God of judgment (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.18">Isa. xxx. 18</reference>), we shall see no reason to despair of relief from him, but all the reason in the world to hope in him, that it will come in due time, in the best time. 2. That if he had not yet seen an end of his troubles, the reason was because he did not thus trust in God and wait for him (<reference osisRef="Job.35.15">v. 15</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Because it is not so,</hi> because thou dost not thus trust in him, therefore the affliction which came at first from love has now displeasure mixed with it. Now God <hi type="italic">has visited</hi> thee <hi type="italic">in his anger,</hi> taking it very ill that thou canst not find in thy heart to trust him, but harbourest such hard misgiving thoughts of him." If there be any mixtures of divine wrath in our afflictions, we may thank ourselves; it is because we do not behave aright under them; we quarrel with God, and are fretful and impatient, and distrustful of the divine Providence. This was Job's case. <hi type="italic">The foolishness of man perverts his way, and</hi> then <hi type="italic">his heart frets against the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.19.3">Prov. xix. 3</reference>. Yet Elihu thinks that Job, being in great extremity, did not know and consider this as he should, that it was his own fault that he was not yet delivered. He concludes therefore that <hi type="italic">Job opens his mouth in vain</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.35.16">v. 16</reference>) in complaining of his grievances and crying for redress, or in justifying himself and clearing up his own innocency; it is all in vain, because he does not trust in God and wait for him, and has not a due regard to him in his afflictions. He had said a great deal, had <hi type="italic">multiplied words,</hi> but all <hi type="italic">without knowledge,</hi> all to no purpose, because he did not encourage himself in God and humble himself before him. It is in vain for us either to appeal to God or to acquit ourselves if we do not study to answer the end for which affliction is sent, and in vain to pray for relief if we do not trust in God; for let not that man who distrusts God <hi type="italic">think that he shall receive any thing from him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.1.7">James i. 7</reference>. Or this may refer to all that Job had said. Having shown the absurdity of some passages in his discourse, he concludes that there were many other passages which were in like manner the fruits of his ignorance and mistake. He did not, as his other friends, condemn him for a hypocrite, but charged him only with Moses's sin, <hi type="italic">speaking unadvisedly with his lips</hi> when his spirit was provoked. When at any time we do so (and who is there that offends not in word?) it is a mercy to be told of it, and we must take it patiently and kindly as Job did, not repeating, but recanting, what we have said amiss.  <chapter eID="Job.35"/> <div eID="gen10139" type="x-p"/>

entries.a0265bbd0f6605cf51e4120db5bf1b7cb1c6d7e9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5245"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 35</title> <div sID="gen7823" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Job.35.1-Job.35.16">Job 35:1-16</reference>.<div eID="gen7823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7824" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5245"/><hi type="bold">2. more than--</hi>rather as in <reference osisRef="Job.9.2">Job 9:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.25.4">25:4</reference>: "I am righteous (literally, my righteousness is) before God." The English Version, however, agrees with <reference osisRef="Job.9.17">Job 9:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.16.12-Job.16.17">16:12-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.27.2-Job.27.6">27:2-6</reference>. <reference osisRef="Job.4.17">Job 4:17</reference> is susceptible of either rendering. Elihu means Job said so, not in so many words, but virtually. <div eID="gen7824" type="x-p"/>
entries.0cbc38e4d2bafdb71a9b55b12bbf9dcaa48b53a9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5246"/><div sID="gen7825" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5246"/>3. Rather, explanatory of "this" in <reference osisRef="Job.35.2">Job 35:2</reference>, "That thou sayest (to thyself, as if a distinct person) What advantage is it (thy integrity) to thee? What profit have I (by integrity) more than (I should have) by my sin?" that is, more than if I had sinned (<reference osisRef="Job.34.9">Job 34:9</reference>). Job had said that the wicked, who use these very words, do not suffer for it (<reference osisRef="Job.21.13-Job.21.15">Job 21:13-15</reference>); whereby he virtually sanctioned their sentiments. The same change of persons from oblique to direct address occurs (<reference osisRef="Job.19.28">Job 19:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.22.17">22:17</reference>). <div eID="gen7825" type="x-p"/>
entries.b3c369d4ad4489628edd6557797b9d8d5808033f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5247"/><div sID="gen7826" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5247"/><hi type="bold">4. companions--</hi>those entertaining like sentiments with thee (<reference osisRef="Job.34.8">Job 34:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.34.36">36</reference>). <div eID="gen7826" type="x-p"/>
entries.df9f290eda496971340d3090c3aff5b0a22ce9b9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5248"/><div sID="gen7827" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5248"/>5-8. Elihu like Eliphaz (<reference osisRef="Job.22.2">Job 22:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.3.12">3, 12</reference>) shows that God is too exalted in nature to be susceptible of benefit or hurt from the righteousness or sin of men respectively; it is themselves that they benefit by righteousness, or hurt by sin.<div eID="gen7827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7828" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">behold the clouds, which are higher than thou--</hi>spoken with irony. Not only are they higher than thou, but thou canst not even reach them clearly with the eye. Yet these are not as high as God's seat. God is therefore too exalted to be dependent on man. Therefore He has no inducement to injustice in His dealings with man. When He afflicts, it must be from a different motive; namely, the good of the sufferer. <div eID="gen7828" type="x-p"/>
entries.457d7719483c316ab0e5be2f4cc6ddf7bc9090df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5251"/><div sID="gen7832" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5251"/>9. (<reference osisRef="Eccl.4.1">Ec 4:1</reference>.) Elihu states in Job's words (Job 24. 12; 30. 20) the difficulty; the "cries" of "the oppressed" not being heard might lead man to think that wrongs are not punished by Him. <div eID="gen7832" type="x-p"/>
entries.244cd03777ef5947b7e8a9468fa9de690fc80b8a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5252"/><div sID="gen7833" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5252"/>10-13. But the reason is that the innocent sufferers often do not humbly seek God for succor; so to their "pride" is to be laid the blame of their ruin; also because (<reference osisRef="Job.35.13-Job.35.16">Job 35:13-16</reference>) they, as Job, instead of waiting God's time in pious trust, are prone to despair of His justice, when it is not immediately visible (<reference osisRef="Job.33.19-Job.33.26">Job 33:19-26</reference>). If the sufferer would apply to God with a humbled, penitent spirit, He would hear.<div eID="gen7833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7834" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Where, &c.--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.2.6">Jr 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.13">Is 51:13</reference>).<div eID="gen7834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7835" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">songs--</hi>of joy at deliverance (<reference osisRef="Ps.42.8">Psa 42:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.149.5">149:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.16.25">Ac 16:25</reference>).<div eID="gen7835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7836" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the night--</hi>unexpectedly (<reference osisRef="Job.34.20">Job 34:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.34.25">25</reference>). Rather, "in calamity." <div eID="gen7836" type="x-p"/>
entries.a0d5379c057f741eb0afd4f9328af78d5726001e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5256"/><div sID="gen7841" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5256"/><hi type="bold">14. Although thou sayest thou shalt not see him--</hi>(as a temporal deliverer; for he did look for a Redeemer after death, <reference osisRef="Job.19.25-Job.19.27">Job 19:25-27</reference>; which passage cannot consistently with Elihu's assertion here be interpreted of "seeing" a temporal "redeemer"), <reference osisRef="Job.7.7">Job 7:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.9.11">9:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.23.3">23:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.8.9">8, 9</reference>; yet, judgment ... ; therefore trust ... But the Hebrew favors Maurer, "How much less (will God ... regard, <reference osisRef="Job.35.13">Job 35:13</reference>), since thou sayest, that He does not regard thee." So in <reference osisRef="Job.4.19">Job 4:19</reference>. Thus Elihu alludes to Job's words (<reference osisRef="Job.19.7">Job 19:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.30.20">30:20</reference>).<div eID="gen7841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7842" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judgment--</hi>that is, thy cause, thy right; as in <reference osisRef="Ps.9.16">Psa 9:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.31.5">Pr 31:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.31.8">8</reference>.<div eID="gen7842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7843" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">trust--</hi>rather, "wait thou" on Him, patiently, until He take up thy cause (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.7">Psa 37:7</reference>). <div eID="gen7843" type="x-p"/>
entries.2582163cb03c83e3a4f43548dfaa3a87a9a237ca: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5257"/><div sID="gen7844" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5257"/>15. As it is, because Job waited not trustingly and patiently (<reference osisRef="Job.35.14">Job 35:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.20.12">Nu 20:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.2">Zep 3:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.7.9">Mi 7:9</reference>), God hath visited ... ; yet still he has not taken (severe) cognizance of the great multitude (English Version wrongly, "extremity") of sins; therefore Job should not complain of being punished with undue severity (<reference osisRef="Job.7.20">Job 7:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.11.6">11:6</reference>). Maurer translates: "Because His anger hath not visited (hath not immediately punished Job for his impious complaints), nor has He taken strict (great) cognizance of his folly (sinful speeches); therefore," &c. For "folly," Umbreit translates with the Rabbins, "multitude." Gesenius reads with the Septuagint and Vulgate needlessly, "transgression." <div eID="gen7844" type="x-p"/>
entries.0de94e25db203edd283327f46f179b9cfa6a7cfc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5258"/><div sID="gen7845" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5258"/>16. Apodosis to <reference osisRef="Job.35.15">Job 35:15</reference>.<div eID="gen7845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7846" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in vain--</hi>rashly. <chapter eID="Job.35"/>

entries.45be374a4cc6058d97f35c9bddd367ad85f514ac: <div eID="gen17675" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen17676" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17677" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17677" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17676" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17678" type="x-p"/> Elihu accuses Job of impious speeches, <reference osisRef="Job.35.1-Job.35.4">Job 35:1-4</reference>. No man can affect God by his iniquity, nor profit him by his righteousness, <reference osisRef="Job.35.5-Job.35.8">Job 35:5-8</reference>. Many are afflicted and oppressed, but few cry to God for help; and, for want of faith, they continue in affliction, <reference osisRef="Job.35.9-Job.35.16">Job 35:9-16</reference>.
entries.50c1ce9ff00b0d0cca5d6eb852f209f952dcd2fe: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen17678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17679" type="x-p"/> My righteousness is more than God's? - This would indeed be a blasphemous saying; but Job never said so, neither directly nor constructively: it would be much better to translate the words צדקי מאל tsidki meel, I am righteous Before God. And Job's meaning most certainly was, "Whatever I am in your sight, I know that in the sight of God I am a righteous man;" and he had a right to assume this character, because God himself had given it to him.
entries.dce5b5125dbcdcffb41acb4244cba4fa65b3973d: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen17679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17680" type="x-p"/> What advantage will it be unto thee? - As if he had said to God, "My righteousness cannot profit thee, nor do I find that it is of any benefit to myself." Or perhaps Elihu makes here a general assertion, which he afterwards endeavors to exemplify: Thou hast been reasoning how it may profit thee, and thou hast said, "What profit shall I have in righteousness more than in sin?"
entries.56c755a642f70fe60ac0f2683758dbe0681b41ae: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen17680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17681" type="x-p"/> I will answer thee - I will show thee the evil of a sinful way, and the benefit of righteousness; and supply what thy friends have omitted in their discourses with thee.
entries.bb07373f193ef68a41a402bc6d45cf2dac932b9c: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen17681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17682" type="x-p"/> Look unto the heavens - These heavens, and their host, God has created: the bare sight of them is sufficient to show thee that God is infinitely beyond thee in wisdom and excellence. <div eID="gen17682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17683" type="x-p"/> Behold the clouds - שחקים shechakim, the ethers, (Vulgate, aethera), from שחק shachak, to contend, fight together: the agitated or conflicting air and light; the strong agitation of these producing both light and heat. Look upon these, consider them deeply, and see and acknowledge the perfections of the Maker.
entries.59c2c2f52a44bef1a54e87220f95ae2a1409aa96: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen17683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17684" type="x-p"/> If thou sinnest - God is not benefited by thy righteousness, nor injured by thy iniquity, howsoever multiplied it may be.
entries.dfda773b60d742989736d302abb57b57ffe63f0b: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen17684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17685" type="x-p"/> Thy wickedness may hurt - It is better to translate this literally: <div eID="gen17685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17686" type="x-p"/> To a man like thyself is thy wickedness: <div eID="gen17686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17687" type="x-p"/> And to the son of man, thy righteousness: <div eID="gen17687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17688" type="x-p"/> That is: - <div eID="gen17688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17689" type="x-p"/> Thou mayest injure thyself and others by thy wickedness, <div eID="gen17689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17690" type="x-p"/> And thou mayest benefit both by thy righteousness; <div eID="gen17690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17691" type="x-p"/> But God thou canst neither hurt nor profit.
entries.65517563907f7faa4d880f4983198a3650f81bd8: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen17691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17692" type="x-p"/> By reason of the multitude - Or rather, "From among the multitude" the oppressed clamor, יזעיקו yaziku: they shout, ישועו yeshavveu, because of the mighty. The wicked rich oppress the wicked poor; these cry aloud because of their oppressors; but they have no relief, because they call not upon God.
entries.1ba2ed630a41edcb29a6b64c8f8d88909a6e8d92: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen17692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17693" type="x-p"/> Where is God my Maker - They have no just apprehension of his being; they do not consider themselves his creatures, or that he who created them still preserves them, and would make them happy if they would pray unto him. <div eID="gen17693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17694" type="x-p"/> Who giveth songs in the night - This is variously translated. "Before whom the high angels give praise in the night." - Chaldee. "Who sets the night-watches." - Septuagint. "Gives meditations in the night." - Syriac and Arabic. "And that shyneth upon us that we might prayse him in the night." - Coverdale. <div eID="gen17694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17695" type="x-p"/> A holy soul has continual communion with God: night and day its happiness is great; and God, from whom it comes, is the continual subject of its songs of praise.
entries.d9fae6e7de373cc37e8dd7a33ed32305681eef15: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen17695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17696" type="x-p"/> Who teacheth us more than the beasts - "The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib; but Israel doth not know me, my people do not consider;" <reference osisRef="Isa.1.3">Isa 1:3</reference>. Beasts, bards, fowls, and in many cases pond-fishes, know and seem thankful to the hand that feeds them; while man, made much more noble than they, gifted with the greatest powers, privileged with the most important benefits, considers not the Lord, nor discerns the operation of his hand. Quadrupeds, reptiles, and fowls, have more gratitude to their masters than man has to his God.
entries.0bb8d606dbbc6d7e88cc626315631c9ae452211c: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen17696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17697" type="x-p"/> There they cry - They bewail their calamities, but sorrow not for the cause of them; they cry against their oppressors, but they call not upon God. <div eID="gen17697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17698" type="x-p"/> Because of the pride of evil men - Or מפני mippeney, from the face, presence, or influence, of the pride of wicked men. They cry for deliverance from the pride of wicked men; but they are not heard, because they cry not to God.
entries.4a7981acd7ce4caf208978b1cb7cf20b01affee0: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen17698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17699" type="x-p"/> Surely God will not hear vanity - He will not attend to such vain cries; they cry from their oppressions, but they cry not to God.
entries.588c864e863a65e3302be069178df59c66298b7a: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen17699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17700" type="x-p"/> Thou sayest thou shalt not see Him - Several MSS. have "Thou shalt not see me," and the Septuagint, and one other, "Thou shalt not see us," but without the points, תשורנו, the original may be read see Him or see Us, the third person singular, or the first person plural. <div eID="gen17700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17701" type="x-p"/> Yet judgment is before him - Rest assured that God has not forgotten either to punish or to save; therefore trust in him; choose to be a monument of his mercy, rather than of his justice.
entries.30ec514657c250490d46c1880055704b19e2fbba: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen17701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17702" type="x-p"/> But - because it is not so - Rather, "But now, because he visiteth not in his anger." This is more literal than the versions generally proposed; and the sense of the place appears to be this: Because vengeance is not speedily executed on an evil work, therefore are the hearts of the children of men set in them to do iniquity. This is, in effect, the charge which Elihu brings against Job.
entries.f21a11483bd2de4be2439828fa750ccb47c38be5: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen17702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17703" type="x-p"/> Therefore doth Job open his mouth in vain - God will execute vengeance when it may best serve the ends of his justice, providence, and mercy. The delay of judgment is not proof that it shall not be executed; nor is the deferring of mercy any proof that God has forgotten to be gracious. <div eID="gen17703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17704" type="x-p"/> He multiplieth words without knowledge - However this may apply to Job, it most certainly applies very strongly and generally to the words, not only of Job's three friends, but to those also of Elihu himself. The contest is frequently a strife of words.  <chapter eID="Job.35"/> <div eID="gen17704" type="x-p"/>

entries.31df858dff12afe48dd2bbf929e313d838e4716c: <reference osisRef="Job.35.1-Job.4.1">Job 35:1-4   1</reference>  Then began Elihu, and said:   2  Dost thou consider this to be right, <div eID="gen8469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8470" type="x-p"/> Sayest thou: my righteousness exceedeth God’s,   3  That thou sayest, what advantage is it to thee, <div eID="gen8470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8471" type="x-p"/> What doth it profit me more than my sin?   4  I will answer thee words, <div eID="gen8471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8472" type="x-p"/> And thy companions with thee. <div eID="gen8472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8473" type="x-p"/> The neutral זאת, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.35.2">Job 35:2</reference></hi>, refers prospectively to כּי־תאמר, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.35.3">Job 35:3</reference></hi>: this that thou sayest. חשׁב with <hi type="italic">acc</hi>. of the obj. and ל of the predicate, as <reference osisRef="Job.33.10">Job 33:10</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Job.13.24">Job 13:24</reference>, and freq. The second interrogative clause, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.35.2">Job 35:2</reference></hi>, is co-ordinate with the first, and the collective thought of this ponderous construction, <reference osisRef="Job.35.2">Job 35:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.35.3">Job 35:3</reference>, is this: Considerest thou this to be right, and thinkest thou on this account to be able to put thy righteousness above the divine, that, as thou maintainest, no righteousness on the side of God corresponds to this thy righteousness, because God makes no distinction between righteousness and the sin of man, and allows the former to go unrewarded? צדקי (for which Olsh. wishes to read צדקתּי, as <reference osisRef="Job.9.27">Job 9:27</reference> אמרתי for אמרי) forms with מאל a substantival clause: <hi type="italic">justitia mea est prae Deo (prae divina</hi>); מן comparative as <reference osisRef="Job.32.2">Job 32:2</reference>, comp. on the matter <reference osisRef="Job.34.5">Job 34:5</reference>, not equivalent to ἀπό as Job 4:17. כי־תאמר is first followed by the <hi type="italic">oratio obliqua:</hi> what it (viz., צדקך) advantageth thee, then by the <hi type="italic">or. directa</hi> (on this change vid., Ew. §338, a): what profit have I (viz., בצדקי), <hi type="italic">prae peccato meo;</hi> this מן is also comparative; the constantly ambiguous combination would be allowable from the fact that, according to the usage of the language, “to obtain profit from anything” is expressed by הועיל בּ, not by הועיל מן. Moreover, <hi type="italic">prae peccato meo</hi> is equivalent to <hi type="italic">plus quam inde quod pecco,</hi> comp. <reference osisRef="Ps.18.24">Psa 18:24</reference>, מעוני, Hos 4:8 אל־עונם. We have already on <reference osisRef="Job.34.9">Job 34:9</reference> observed that Job has not directly said (he cites it, <reference osisRef="Job.21.15">Job 21:15</reference>, as the saying of the ungodly) what Elihu in <reference osisRef="Job.35.3">Job 35:3</reference> puts into his mouth, but as an inference it certainly is implied in such utterances as Job 9:22. Elihu’s polemic against Job and his companions (רעיך are not the three, as lxx and Jer. translate, but the אנשׁי און, to whom Job is likened by such words as <reference osisRef="Job.34.8">Job 34:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.34.36">Job 34:36</reference>) is therefore not unauthorized; especially since he assails the conclusion together with its premises. In the second strophe the vindication of the conclusion is now refuted.
entries.474842505273a13548300369df77ee8653033a10: <reference osisRef="Job.35.5-Job.8.5">Job 35:5-8   5</reference>  Look towards heaven and see, <div eID="gen8473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8474" type="x-p"/> And behold the ethereal heights: they are high above thee.   6  If thou sinnest, what dost thou effect with Him? <div eID="gen8474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8475" type="x-p"/> And if thy transgressions are many, what doest thou to Him?   7  If thou art righteous, what dost thou give Him, <div eID="gen8475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8476" type="x-p"/> Or what doth He take from thy hand?   8  To man like thee thy godlessness availeth, <div eID="gen8476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8477" type="x-p"/> And to thee, a son of man, thy righteousness. <div eID="gen8477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8478" type="x-p"/> Towards heaven he is to direct his gaze, to obtain from the height of heaven a notion of the exaltation of God who dwells above the heavens. The combination הבּיט וראה is like <reference osisRef="Ps.80.15">Psa 80:15</reference> and freq. שׁחקים (שׁחק, Arab. <hi type="italic">sḥq</hi>, to rub in pieces, make thin, therefore the opposite of עבים) are the thin transparent strata of the atmosphere above the hanging clouds. מן after גּבהּ denotes the height that is on the opposite side to the beholder. From the exaltation of God it is then further inferred that it is impossible to exercise any human influence upon Him, by which He might suffer. The pointing wavers here between תּפעל (the common <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. form) and תּפעל(as a contraction of תּפעל after the form אזעם, Num 23:8). Human wrong or right doing neither diminishes nor increases His blessedness; injury or advantage is only on the side of man, from whom it proceeds. Others, whom his conduct affect, are not included in <reference osisRef="Job.35.8">Job 35:8</reference> : righteous or ungodly doing, Elihu means to say, as such and with its consequences, belongs solely to the doer himself, the man “like thee” (לאישׁ with <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>, כּמוך with <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>), the son of man, i.e., man, capable of evil as of good, and who always, after deciding in favour of the latter or the former, determines his fortune or misfortune, in distinction from God, who ever remains unchangeably the same in His perfect righteousness. What Elihu here says we have already heard from Eliphaz, Job 22:2., and Job even expresses himself similarly in <reference osisRef="Job.7.20">Job 7:20</reference>; but to Elihu’s mind it all becomes for Job new and powerful motives to quiet submission, for what objection should Job raise in justification of his complaints concerning his affliction against such sentiments as these, that goodness bears its reward and evil its punishment in itself, and that God’s reward of goodness is not a work of indebtedness, nor His punishment of evil a work of necessity? Before such truth he must really hold his peace.
entries.2c6b8dcab8ec2a1ae921f689ae3844486a7b633d: <reference osisRef="Job.35.9-Job.13.9">Job 35:9-13   9</reference>  By reason of the multitude of oppressions they raise a cry, <div eID="gen8478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8479" type="x-p"/> They call for help by reason of the arm of the great, 10  But none saith: Where is Eloah my Creator, <div eID="gen8479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8480" type="x-p"/> Who giveth songs of praise in the night, 11  Who teacheth us by the beasts of the earth, <div eID="gen8480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8481" type="x-p"/> And maketh us wise by the fowls of heaven? 12  Then they cry, yet He answereth not, <div eID="gen8481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8482" type="x-p"/> Because of the pride of evil men. 13  Vanity alone God heareth not, <div eID="gen8482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8483" type="x-p"/> And the Almighty observeth it not. <div eID="gen8483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8484" type="x-p"/> In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.35.9">Job 35:9</reference></hi> the accentuation of מרוב with <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi>, according to which Dachselt interprets: <hi type="italic">prae multitudine (oppressionum) oppressi clamabunt,</hi> is erroneous; it is to be written מרב, as everywhere else, and this (according to Codd. and the editions of Jablonski, Majus, Michaelis, and others) is to be accented with <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>, which is followed by עשׁוּקים with a vicarious <hi type="italic">Munach: prae multitudine oppressionum</hi> (עשׁוקים like <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.4.1">Ecc 4:1</reference></hi>, and probably also <reference osisRef="Amos.3.9">Amo 3:9</reference>) <hi type="italic">edunt clamorem</hi> (<hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. in the intensive <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> signification, as e.g., הזנה, to commit fornication, Hos 4:10). On זרוע, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.35.9">Job 35:9</reference></hi>; רבּים are the great or lords (Arab. <hi type="italic">arbâb</hi>). The <hi type="italic">plur</hi>. with a general subj. is followed by the <hi type="italic">sing</hi>. in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.35.10">Job 35:10</reference></hi>: and no one says (exactly as in האמר, <reference osisRef="Job.34.31">Job 34:31</reference>). Elihu weakens the doubt expressed by Job in <reference osisRef="Job.24.12">Job 24:12</reference>, that God allows injustice to prevail, and oppressed innocence remains without vindication. The failure of the latter arises from the fact of the sufferers complaining, but not seeking earnestly the only true helper, God their maker (עשׂים, intensive <hi type="italic">plur.,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Isa.22.11">Isa 22:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.54.5">Isa 54:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.149.2">Psa 149:2</reference>), who gives (to which may be compared a passage of the Edda: “Wuodan gives songs to the Scalds”) songs (זמרות, from the onomatopoetic זמר) in the night, i.e., who in the night of sorrow puts songs of praise concerning the dawning light of help into the mouth of the sufferers. The singing of the glory of the nightly heavens (Stick., Hahn) is to be as little thought of as the music of the spheres; the night is, as <reference osisRef="Job.34.20">Job 34:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.34.25">Job 34:25</reference>, the time of unexpectedly sudden change. <div eID="gen8484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8485" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Job.35.11">Job 35:11</reference> most expositors (last of all Schlottm.) take the two מן as comparative. Elihu would then, since he feels the absence of the asking after this God on the part of the sufferers, mean the conscious relation in which He has placed us to Himself, and in accordance with which the sufferer should not merely instinctively complain, but humbly bow himself and earnestly offer up prayer. But according to <reference osisRef="Job.12.7">Job 12:7</reference> (comp. <reference osisRef="Prov.6.6">Pro 6:6</reference>, וחכם), it is to be translated: who teaches (מלּפנוּ = מאלּפנוּ, comp. <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.40">2Sa 22:40</reference>, <hi type="italic">Psalter</hi> i. 160) us from the beasts of the earth (so that from them as a means of instruction teaching comes to us), and makes us wise from the birds of heaven. The <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. interchanging with the <hi type="italic">part</hi>. better accords with this translation, according to which <reference osisRef="Job.35.11">Job 35:11</reference> is a continuation of the assertion of a divine instruction, by means of the animal creation; the thought also suits the connection better, for of the many things that may be learned from the animal creation, prayer here comes under consideration, - the lions roar, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.21">Psa 104:21</reference>; the thirsty cattle cry to God, <reference osisRef="Joel.1.20">Joe 1:20</reference>; the ravens call upon God, Psa 147:9. It we now determine the collective thought of <reference osisRef="Job.35.10">Job 35:10</reference>, that affliction does not drive most men to God the almighty Helper, who will be humbly entreated for help: it is more natural to take שׁם (vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.23.7">Job 23:7</reference>) in the sense of then (τότε), than, with reference to the scene of oppression, in the sense of there (lxx, Jer.: <hi type="italic">ibi</hi>). The division of the verse is correct, and H. B. Starcke has correctly interpreted<hi type="italic">: Tunc clamabunt (sed non respondebit) propter superbiam (insolentiam) malorum</hi>. מפּני is not to be connected with יענה in the sense of <hi type="italic">non exaudiet et servabit,</hi> by which <hi type="italic">constr. praegnans</hi> one would expect מן, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.22">Psa 22:22</reference>, instead of מפני, nor in the sense of <hi type="italic">non exaudiet propter</hi> (Hirz., Schlottm.), for the arrogant רעים are not those who complain unheard: but, as the connection shows, those from whom the occasion of complaint proceeds. Therefore: not allowing themselves to be driven to God by oppression, they cry then, without, however, being heard of God, by reason of the arrogance of evil men which they have to endure. <reference osisRef="Job.35.13">Job 35:13</reference> gives the reason of their obtaining no answer: Only emptiness (i.e., mere motion of the lips without the true spirit of prayer) God heareth not, and the Almighty observeth it not. Hahn wrongly denies אך the significations <hi type="italic">certo</hi> and <hi type="italic">verumtamen;</hi> but we prefer the restrictive signification (sheer emptiness or hollowness) which proceeds from the affirmative primary signification<note placement="foot">Vid., Hupfeld in the <hi type="italic">Zeitschr. für Kunde des Morgenl.</hi> ii. 441f.</note> here, to the adversative (nevertheless emptiness), since the adversative thought, <hi type="italic">verumtamen non exaudit,</hi> has found its expression already in ולא יענה.
entries.3a99655f3003987f103e96108b3cd1afcf3bd724: <reference osisRef="Job.35.14-Job.16.14">Job 35:14-16 14</reference>  Although thou sayest, thou seest Him not: <div eID="gen8485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8486" type="x-p"/> The cause lieth before Him, and thou mayest wait for Him. 15  Now, then, if His wrath hath not yet punished, <div eID="gen8486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8487" type="x-p"/> Should He not be well acquainted with sullenness? 16  While Job openeth his mouth without reason, <div eID="gen8487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8488" type="x-p"/> Without knowledge multiplieth words. <div eID="gen8488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8489" type="x-p"/> The address is not direct to Job exclusively, for it here treats first of the acts of injustice which prevail among men and remain apparently unpunished; but to Job, however, also, so far as he has, <reference osisRef="Job.23.8-Job.23.10">Job 23:8-10</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Job.19.7">Job 19:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.30.20">Job 30:20</reference>, thus complained concerning his prayer being unanswered. אף כּי signifies elsewhere <hi type="italic">quanto minus,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.4.19">Job 4:19</reference>, or also <hi type="italic">quanto magis,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.11">Pro 15:11</reference>, but nowhere <hi type="italic">quanto minus si</hi> (Hirz., Hlgst.) or <hi type="italic">quanto magis si</hi> (Hahn), also not <reference osisRef="Ezek.15.5">Eze 15:5</reference>, where it signifies <hi type="italic">etiamne quum.</hi> As it can, however, naturally signify <hi type="italic">etiam quum,</hi> it can also signify <hi type="italic">etiamsi, etsi</hi>, as here and Neh 9:18. This <hi type="italic">quamvis dicas</hi> (<hi type="italic">opineris</hi>) is followed by the <hi type="italic">oratio obliqua,</hi> as Job 35:3. The relation of the matter - says the conclusion, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.35.14">Job 35:14</reference></hi> - is other than thou thinkest: the matter to be decided lies before Him, is therefore well known to Him, and thou mightest only wait for Him (חולל instead of יחל or הוחיל only here, comp. <reference osisRef="Ps.37.7">Psa 37:7</reference>, והתחולל לו); the decision, though it pass by, will not fail. In <reference osisRef="Job.35.15">Job 35:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.35.15">Job 35:15</reference> is taken by most modern commentators as antecedent to <reference osisRef="Job.35.16">Job 35:16</reference>, in which case, apart from the distortions introduced, two interpretations are possible: (1) However now, because His (God’s) wrath does not visit ... Job opens his mouth; (2) However now, because He (God) does not visit his (Job’s) wrath (comp. on this reference of the אפּו to Job, <reference osisRef="Job.18.4">Job 18:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.36.13">Job 36:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.36.18">Job 36:18</reference>)...Job opens, etc. That a clause with a confirmatory כי is made to precede its principal clause is not without example, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.14">Gen 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.17">Gen 3:17</reference>; but in connection with this arrangement the verb is accustomed always, in the principal clause or in the conclusion, to stand prominent (so that consequently we should expect ויפצה איוב), although in Arabic this position of the words, ואיוב יפצה, and in fact Arab. <hi type="italic">fâyûb</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">wâyûb</hi> (in connection with a difference of the subj. in the antecedent and in the conclusion, vid., De Sacy, <hi type="italic">Gramm. Arabe,</hi> §1201, 2), is regular. Therefore for a long time I thought that <reference osisRef="Job.35.15">Job 35:15</reference> was to be taken interrogatively: And now (ועתּה as logical inference and conclusion, which is here its most probable function, Ew. §353, <hi type="italic">b</hi>) should His wrath not punish (פּקד as absolute as <reference osisRef="Job.31.14">Job 31:14</reference>), and should He not take notice, etc., כּי interrogative as <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.20">1Sa 24:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.1">1Sa 28:1</reference>; 1Ki 11:22, as הכי (is it so that, or: should it be so that), <reference osisRef="Job.6.22">Job 6:22</reference>, and freq., in connection with which, what is said on <reference osisRef="Gen.21.7">Gen 21:7</reference> concerning the modal use of the <hi type="italic">praet</hi>. might be compared on the two <hi type="italic">praett</hi>. But by this rendering the connection of <reference osisRef="Job.35.16">Job 35:16</reference> with what precedes is awkward. Ewald has given the correct rendering (apart from the misunderstanding of פּשׁ): Therefore, because His wrath has not yet punished, He does not know much about foolishness! <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.35.15">Job 35:15</reference></hi> requires to be taken as the conclusion to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.35.15">Job 35:15</reference></hi>, yet not as an exclamation, but as an interrogative. The interrogative use of ולא is not unusual, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.1">2Sa 20:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.43">Eze 16:43</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.47">Eze 16:47</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.56">Eze 16:56</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.27">Eze 32:27</reference>; and just as here, this interrogative ולא is found after a hypothetical antecedent clause, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.9">1Sa 20:9</reference>; Exo 8:22. <div eID="gen8489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8490" type="x-p"/> In connection with this interrogative rendering of <reference osisRef="Job.35.15">Job 35:15</reference>, it still remains questionable whether it refers to Job’s sin, or sin which prevails among men. The theme of this third speech of Elihu requires the latter reference, although perhaps not without a side-glance at Job’s won arrogant behaviour. The translation shows how suitably <reference osisRef="Job.35.16">Job 35:16</reference> is connected with what precedes: <reference osisRef="Job.35.16">Job 35:16</reference> is a circumstantial clause, or, if one is not willing to take it as a subordinate clause, but prefers to take it as standing on a level with <reference osisRef="Job.35.15">Job 35:15</reference>, an adversative clause attached with <hi type="italic">Waw</hi>, as is frequently the case: but (nevertheless) Job ... ; פּצה פּה of opening the mouth in derision, as <reference osisRef="Lam.2.16">Lam 2:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.3.46">Lam 3:46</reference>; הבל is the <hi type="italic">acc</hi>. of closer definition to it (= בּהבל), and the הכבּיר, which occurs only here and <reference osisRef="Job.36.31">Job 36:31</reference>, signifies without distinction <hi type="italic">magnificare</hi> and <hi type="italic">multiplicare:</hi> Job multiplies high emotional words. As this יכבּיר is, so to speak, Hebraeo-Arabic (Arab. <hi type="italic">akbara</hi>), so is <reference osisRef="Job.35.15">Job 35:15</reference> full of Arabisims: (1) The combination אין פּקד, which has not its like in the Hebrew language (whether it be originally intended as relative or not: <hi type="italic">non est quod visitaverit,</hi> Ew. §321, <hi type="italic">b</hi>), corresponds to the popular Arabic use of <hi type="italic">lys</hi> for <hi type="italic">lâ</hi>, Ges. <hi type="italic">Thes</hi>. i. 82, <hi type="italic">b</hi>; probably אין has the value of an intensive negation (Carey: not at all). (2) The combination ידע בּ, to know about anything, to take knowledge of anything (differently <reference osisRef="Job.12.9">Job 12:9</reference>, but comp. <reference osisRef="Job.24.12">Job 24:12</reference> on the idea), is like the Arab. construction of the verb <hi type="italic">( alima</hi> with <hi type="italic">bi</hi> (concerning) or <hi type="italic">bianna</hi> (because that) of the obj.; מאד (on this vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.31.12">Psa 31:12</reference>) belongs not to בפשׁ (which is indeed possible), but, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.139.14">Psa 139:14</reference>, to ידע. (3) פּשׁ is especially to be explained from the Arabic. The signification a multitude (Jewish expositors, after פּוּשׁ, <hi type="italic">Niph. se diffundere,</hi> <reference osisRef="Nah.3.18">Nah 3:18</reference>) is not suitable; the signification evil (lxx, Jer., and others: פשׁ = פשׁע) presents a forcibly mutilated word, and moreover one devoid of significance in this connection; whereas the Arab. <hi type="italic">fšš</hi> (but not in its derivatives, <hi type="italic">fashsh</hi>, empty-headed; <hi type="italic">fâshûsh</hi>, empty-headedness, imbecility, with its metaphorical sense) indicates a development of signification which leads to the desired end, especially in the Syro-Arabic usage most natural here. The Arab. verb <hi type="italic">fšš</hi> (פשׁשׁ, cogn. Arab. <hi type="italic">fšr</hi>, <hi type="italic">frš</hi>, to extend, <hi type="italic">expandere</hi>) is used originally of water (<hi type="italic">fashsh el - mâ</hi>): to overflow its dam, to overflow its banks, whence a valley by the lake of <hi type="italic">el-Hîgâne</hi>, into which the waters of the lake flow after the winter rains, is called <hi type="italic">el - mefeshsh ;</hi> then of a leathern bottle: to run out (<hi type="italic">tarf mefshûsh</hi>, an emptied bottle), of a tumour (<hi type="italic">waram</hi>): to disperse, disappear, and tropically of anger (<hi type="italic">el - chulq</hi>): to break forth, vent itself on anything, hence the phrase: dost thou make me a <hi type="italic">mefeshshe</hi> (an object for the venting) of thine anger? From this Arab. <hi type="italic">fšš</hi> (distinct from Arab. <hi type="italic">faš med.</hi> <hi type="italic">Waw</hi>, to swim on the surface, trop. to be above, not to allow one’s self to be kept down, and <hi type="italic">med. Je,</hi> comp. פושׁ, <reference osisRef="Hab.1.8">Hab 1:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.11">Jer 50:11</reference>, Mal 4:2, signifies to be proud) is פּשׁ, formed after the forms בּד, מד, מס, a synon. of זדון, or even of עברה in the signification of excessive haughtiness, pride that bursts forth violently.<note placement="foot">The signification <hi type="italic">expandere</hi> also underlies the noun <hi type="italic">fishshe</hi>, the lungs (in Egypt.); the signification <hi type="italic">discutere</hi> (especially <hi type="italic">carminare</hi>, to card wool), which the Talmud. פשׁפשׁ also has, is only a shade of the same signification; the origin of the trop. signification <hi type="italic">fatuum esse</hi> is clear from <hi type="italic">'gaus fashûsh ,</hi> empty nuts. The rice from the Palestine valley of <hi type="italic">Hûle</hi>, it is somewhere said, is worse than the Egyptian, because (what is a fault in the East) in cooking <hi type="italic">tufeshfish</hi>, i.e., it bursts, breaks in pieces (comp. on the other hand: if the seed for sowing sinks to the bottom when put into water, it is good; if it swims on the surface, <hi type="italic">jefûsh</hi>, it is bad). The <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> of this <hi type="italic">fashsha</hi> signifies to cause the water to overflow, trop. <hi type="italic">fashshasha qalbahu</hi>, he gave air to his heart, i.e., he revealed a secret which burdened him. A proverb says: the market (with its life and changing scenes) is a <hi type="italic">feshshâsh</hi> of cares, i.e., consoles a trouble heart. In the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. one says in like manner proverbially, <hi type="italic">el - bukâ jufishsh</hi>, weeping removes the anguish of the soul. - Wetzst.</note> <div eID="gen8490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8491" type="x-p"/> Thus, even at the close of this third speech of Elihu, the Arabic, and in fact Syro-Arabic colouring, common to this section with the rest of the book, is confirmed; while, on the other hand, we miss the bold, original figures which up to <reference osisRef="Job.31.1">Job 31:1</reference> followed like waves one upon another, and we perceive a deficiency of skill, as now and then between Koheleth and Solomon. The chief thought of the speech we have also heard already from the three friends and Job himself. That the piety of the pious profits himself without involving God in any obligation to him, Eliphaz has already said, Job 22:2.; and that prayer that is heard in time of need and the unanswered cry of the godly and the ungodly are distinct, Job said, Job 27:9. Elihu, however, deprives these thoughts of their hitherto erroneous application. If piety gives nothing to God which He ought to reward, Job dare not regard his affliction, mysterious as it is to him, as unjust; and if the godly do not directly experience the avenging wrath of God on the haughtiness of their oppressors, the question, whether then their prayer for help is of the right kind, is more natural than the complain of a want of justice in God’s government of the world. Job is silent also after this speech. It does not contain the right consolation; it contains, however, censure which he ought humbly to receive. It touches his heart. But whether it touches the heart of the idea of the book, is another question.  <chapter eID="Job.35"/> <div eID="gen8491" type="x-p"/>

                        </ns0:gap>e God and justifie themselves upon all occasions; and partly, that he might awaken <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> to a more serious review of his former assertions by representing to him whose cause he pleaded and who were his consederates and colleagues in this Opinion.</ns0:note> with thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 22. 12.</ns0:note> Look unto the heavens, and see, and behold <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">

And this infinite distance between God and thee, should cause thee to think and speak more modestly and reverently of that glorious Majesty.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6. If thou sinnest, what doest thou against him <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Thy sins do him no hurt, and therefore thy righteousness brings him no benefit, as it follows.</ns0:note>? or <ns0:hi>if</ns0:hi> thy transgressions be multiplied, what doest thou un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to him?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 22. 3. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 16. 2. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 11. 35.</ns0:note> If thou be righteous what givest thou him? or what receiveth he of thine hand <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">He gaineth nothing by it, nor can indeed receive any good from thee, because all thy good comes from him. And therefore thou hast no reason to boast of, nor to upbraid God with thy Piety, which is much to thy advantage, but nothing to his.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8. Thy wickedness <ns0:hi>may hurt</ns0:hi> a man as thou <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">If God were such an one as thou art, he might have benefit or hurt by thine actions: but being an infinite, independent and self<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sufficient being, he is far exalted above all thy good or evil.</ns0:note>, and thy righteousness <ns0:hi>may profit</ns0:hi> the son of man.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9. By reason of the multitude <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>greatness.</ns0:hi> This Verse is supposed to contain an argument to prove what he said, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 8. that one Mans wickedness may hurt another. Or, 2. that which <ns0:hi>Job</ns0:hi> had alledg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed, Chap. 24. 12. and which might seem to reflect upon God's Providence. This therefore <ns0:hi>Elihu</ns0:hi> repeats in this Verse, and an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />swereth in the following.</ns0:note> of oppressions, they make <ns0:hi>the oppressed</ns0:hi> to cry <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Not onely to murmur and complain, but to cry out by reason of sore oppression, and to cry to the Op<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pressours, or others for pity and help.</ns0:note>: they cry out by reason of the arm of the mighty <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Because their Oppres<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sours are too strong for them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:416" />10. But none <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Few or none (for few are oft can <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>

All which were Obligations up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on them to praise God and pray to him, and depend upon him, and aggravations of their gross neglect of God.                         <ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rality of Persons in the Divine Essence, of which see on <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 1. 26.</ns0:note>? who giveth <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">P<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">

Or rather 2. properly, as this word is always used in <ns0:hi>Job</ns0:hi> one place excepted which is doubtful, to wit, Chap. 36. 20. which he may mention rather than the day; either because oppressed Persons who in the day time are cruelly used by their Oppressours are per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mitted to rest in the night: or because the hand and mercy of God is more manifest in the preservation, and rest, and sleep of the night, than in the Blessings of the day which are procured by Mans industry: or because the day is the time of Action, the Night of contemplation, when we do and ought to remember God's Mercies with thanksgiving; compare <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 42. 8. & 119. 62.</ns0:note>!</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11. Who teacheth us more then the beasts <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">This is mentioned as a further aggravation of Mens neglect of God in their misery. And therefore it ill becometh them to lye like Brute-creatures, roaring and crying out in their miseries without taking any notice of God in way of Prayer or Praise; and if they do so, it is no wonder if God takes no notice of them.</ns0:note> of the earth, and maketh us wiser then the fowls of heaven.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12. There <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>Then,</ns0:hi> as this Particle is used, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 14. 5. <ns0:hi>Eccles.</ns0:hi> 3. 17. <ns0:hi>Zeph.</ns0:hi> 1. 14 In that time or condition.</ns0:note> they cry, (but none giveth answer) because of the pride of evil men <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Either 1. of the Oppressours.                         </ns0:gap>. 11. 11.</ns0:note> Surely God will not hear vanity <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Either 1. vain and light Persons, that have no true Wisdom or solid Piety in them, but are wholly addicted to vain and worldly things, rejoycing immoderately when they have them, and crying out for want of them, as here they do.
